title: 🎓 Clo Academic Webinar Series: Pattern Power-Up
description:
When This Workshop Took Place: Apr 10, 2026

Who This Workshop is For: Academic (Faculties & Students)

In this session from CLO's Academic Webinar Series, designed to bridge the gap between the classroom and the digital transformation in the global fashion industry, you'll learn how to work with avatars, create patterns from scratch, and bring garments to life in CLO simulation environment.
This session was conducted for academics (professors & instructors) and was also open to students to join and learn together.
Whether you're a fashion student, educator, or industry professional new to digital pattern making, this webinar walks you through every foundational step: from customizing your avatar's measurements to drafting, tracing, and constructing a basic bodice block entirely within CLO.

📌 What You'll Learn:
How to set up and customize avatars using Avatar Editor and Avatar Joints
How to take accurate body measurements (Basic Tape, Surface Tape, Linear, and Height)
How to navigate CLO's 2D Pattern Window
How to import and trace physical pattern pieces into digital patterns
How to use pattern drafting tools: French curves, rulers, fold lines, offset outlines, and more
How to construct a basic bodice block from real paper patterns

🧵 Part of an ongoing webinar series covering the full CLO workflow: Avatar → Pattern → Sew → Design Ideation → Materials → Production Ready.

markdown_content: ## Webinar Overview: CLO Academic Webinar Series “Pattern Power-Up” This section introduces the CLO Academic Webinar Series for academics, explaining the webinar’s focus areas: digital workflow, tools for pattern making/garment construction, industry readiness, and how 3D and AI relate to CLO. The “Pattern Power-Up” session is part of a broader CLO webinar series planned for academics at regular intervals. The goal is to bridge what is taught in classrooms with the digital transformation happening globally in the fashion industry. The session emphasizes the digital workflow used in industry and the features/tools needed to achieve it. The webinar series aims to cover: - **Curriculum integration**: How CLO (as an ecosystem) can be incorporated into academic curriculum, focusing on tools for **pattern making** and **garment construction**, and other related subjects. - **Industry readiness**: Following industry digital workflows so students can make **informed decisions**. - **Technology trends with 3D and AI**: CLO’s view that **3D design is foundational for AI**, enabling tools that enhance creativity and efficiency. - **Academic use cases / success stories**: Highlighting success when faculties incorporate the CLO ecosystem into academic curricula. The planned macro-level webinar lineup includes topics such as: - Economic growth cycle (mentioned as part of the lineup) - Academic research operations and their role in business/product development - Production readiness (e.g., auto-populating **point of measurement**, **bill of material**, and creating **tech packs**) - Student presentation of 3D renders/designs in final portfolios ## Part 1: Digital Workflow Foundation — Avatars in CLO This section explains what **avatars** are in CLO and how they replace physical mannequins for 3D garment design, draping, and fitting. It also covers avatar types and key adjustment controls (joints, measurements, poses, and custom sizing). In traditional fashion education, **physical mannequins** support teaching **fit, drape, and pattern making**. In CLO, the digital equivalent is **avatars**. ### What are avatars? **Avatars** are highly realistic, customizable virtual models used as the foundation for **3D garment design**, **draping**, and **fitting**. CLO provides multiple avatar categories, including: - **Fabric** avatars - **Female**, **male**, **teens**, **kids**, and **baby** avatars - Various **sizes** and **ethnicities** - **Mannequins** and **shapes** within CLO ### Avatar customization options Key avatar components and controls include: - **Granular sliders (fast body adjustment)** Adjust basic **height/weight** and specific **waist**, **bust**, and **hip** circumferences. The presenter notes that customizing a body type “takes seconds” compared to padding a physical dress form. - **Avatar joints (biomechanical rigging)** Avatars can be inspected in **X-ray/skeleton view**. They are rigged with **biomechanical joints**, enabling joint-by-joint adjustment based on pose or fit needs. - **Avatar measurements (digital measuring tape)** Yellow lines represent a digital tape measure. Instead of guessing, students can view **precise industry-standard points of measure** directly on the 3D body. Students can verify avatar dimensions while grading patterns to maintain mathematical accuracy. - **Avatar poses (for dynamic presentation)** Because avatars have joints, they can be posed using **preset pose options** for more dynamic final portfolio presentations. ### Custom sizes via Avatar Editor With **Avatar Editor**, students can enter custom measurements for attributes such as: - **Head** - **Hand** - **Hip dips** - **Breast shape** A key behavior described is that the editor uses **mass control** and automatically adjusts **unassigned measurements** to maintain natural body shapes. After customization, students can save the result as an **avatar size file** and reuse it for the same avatar profile. ## Part 2: Measuring Avatars in CLO (Tape Measure & Circumference Tools) This section covers the measurement tools used to capture avatar dimensions in CLO, including tape measurement types and circumference measurement modes. It also lists the measurements needed to draft a shirt block. Students can take avatar measurements and apply them to draft patterns. CLO provides multiple measurement tools, including four tape-measure types and circumference tools. ### Tape measure tool types (4) 1. **Basic tape measure** Measures the **linear length** of a desired part on the avatar surface (e.g., across front). 2. **Surface tape measure** Measures length **following the curves** of the avatar surface (useful for measurements like **bust width**). 3. **Linear avatar tape** Considers **linear length** and is not necessarily constrained to the surface curves. 4. **Height measurement** Measures the height of a specific avatar point from **ground level**. ### Circumference measure tool types (2) 1. **Basic circumference measure** Considers the linear length and does not incorporate body curves. 2. **Surface circumference measure** Measures **body topology** so all curves are incorporated into the circumference value. ### Example: shirt block measurements To draft a **shirt block**, the presenter lists these necessary measurements: - **Back neck** - **Armhole** (presented as “arm silent waist” in the transcript; intended as armhole/related arm measurements) - **Waist** - **Short length** or **full length** - **Sleeve opening** - **Across front** - **Chest** - **Hem opening** ### Measurement workflow example (default avatar) - Using **basic circumference tape**, measure: - **Full chest** - **Full waist** - **Full neck** - Using **basic tape measure**, measure: - **Full length** (described as from HSP to sleeve length) - Note: holding **Shift** makes the tool follow a specific reference line. - Measure **across front** - Measure **biceps circumference** - Measure **sleeve length** and sleeve opening-related values ## Part 3: Tool Digitization (French Curve) for CLO Pattern Drafting This section explains how to digitize physical pattern-making tools (e.g., **French curve**) by importing a top-view image, scaling it with reference measurements, and tracing it into an editable curve shape for use in CLO. To convert physical/manual pattern-making tools into digital equivalents for pattern drafting, CLO uses a digitization approach. ### Digitization inputs and setup - Ideally, you need a **top picture/top view** of the tool with a **transparent background** (or prepared for import). - You also need a **reference measurement** to scale the graphic. In the example: - The reference length is stated as approximately **8.75 inches**. - The tool image is imported into CLO as a **graphic**. - A **pattern** is created first, and the graphic is added to that pattern. - The graphic is resized to match the reference measurement, with attention to **units of measurement**. ### Tracing and preparing the curve - The digitized tool is traced as an **internal shape**. - It is “cut out” as a **pattern**. - Curve points (e.g., French curve points) can be modified individually. - The result is saved as a **garbage file** for further use in **short block construction**. ## Part 4: Drafting a Shirt Body Block in CLO (Back & Front) This section provides a step-by-step CLO pattern drafting workflow for a **shirt body block**, including constructing back and front neckline/armhole geometry using edit tools, offsets, internal polygon connections, and curvature editing (Bezier handles). The session demonstrates drafting a **short pattern** including: - **Body** - **Sleeve** (later in the process) - **Collar** - **Yoke** (later) - **Paru’ll cover collar yoke** (as stated; intended to include collar/yoke construction workflow) ### Use the recorded avatar measurements The same avatar measurements are reused for drafting. ### Create the back pattern 1. Start with a **right-angle rule** to create a **rectangular pattern piece** (pattern paper equivalent). 2. Use **Edit Pattern** to **offset internal lines** to mark key construction levels (e.g., back-neck drop actions). 3. Cut off to the desired outline (described as adjusting for the pattern floor/area). 4. Mark levels for: - **Neck** - **Chest** - **Waist** - **Hem** 5. Adjust the **neck level** length to match **neck width**, then square lines using **Add Perpendicular Internal Line** to create the neck curve baseline. 6. Mark **one-fourth of the chest measurement** on the chest line using **Add Point Split Line** (type measurement). 7. Square perpendicular lines on both sides from created points. 8. Create **shoulder drop level** using **Offset as Internal Line** (based on the back neck position). 9. Create the **across back line** by using **Distribute Internal Line between segments**. 10. Mark **cross back measurement** on the across back line and square to define the shoulder point. 11. Use **Internal Polygon** to connect points and form the basic shape. 12. Move a point slightly to define **armhole depth**. 13. Create armhole/neck curves using the **digitized French curve tool**: - Use **2D toggle** → **Garment Rendering Style**

chunks.title: 🎓 Clo Academic Webinar Series: Pattern Power-Up
chunks.content: ## Webinar Overview: CLO Academic Webinar Series “Pattern Power-Up” This section introduces the CLO Academic Webinar Series for academics, explaining the webinar’s focus areas: digital workflow, tools for pattern making/garment construction, industry readiness, and how 3D and AI relate to CLO. The “Pattern Power-Up” session is part of a broader CLO webinar series planned for academics at regular intervals. The goal is to bridge what is taught in classrooms with the digital transformation happening globally in the fashion industry. The session emphasizes the digital workflow used in industry and the features/tools needed to achieve it. The webinar series aims to cover: - **Curriculum integration**: How CLO (as an ecosystem) can be incorporated into academic curriculum, focusing on tools for **pattern making** and **garment construction**, and other related subjects. - **Industry readiness**: Following industry digital workflows so students can make **informed decisions**. - **Technology trends with 3D and AI**: CLO’s view that **3D design is foundational for AI**, enabling tools that enhance creativity and efficiency. - **Academic use cases / success stories**: Highlighting success when faculties incorporate the CLO ecosystem into academic curricula. The planned macro-level webinar lineup includes topics such as: - Economic growth cycle (mentioned as part of the lineup) - Academic research operations and their role in business/product development - Production readiness (e.g., auto-populating **point of measurement**, **bill of material**, and creating **tech packs**) - Student presentation of 3D renders/designs in final portfolios ## Part 1: Digital Workflow Foundation — Avatars in CLO This section explains what **avatars** are in CLO and how they replace physical mannequins for 3D garment design, draping, and fitting. It also covers avatar types and key adjustment controls (joints, measurements, poses, and custom sizing). In traditional fashion education, **physical mannequins** support teaching **fit, drape, and pattern making**. In CLO, the digital equivalent is **avatars**. ### What are avatars? **Avatars** are highly realistic, customizable virtual models used as the foundation for **3D garment design**, **draping**, and **fitting**. CLO provides multiple avatar categories, including: - **Fabric** avatars - **Female**, **male**, **teens**, **kids**, and **baby** avatars - Various **sizes** and **ethnicities** - **Mannequins** and **shapes** within CLO ### Avatar customization options Key avatar components and controls include: - **Granular sliders (fast body adjustment)** Adjust basic **height/weight** and specific **waist**, **bust**, and **hip** circumferences. The presenter notes that customizing a body type “takes seconds” compared to padding a physical dress form. - **Avatar joints (biomechanical rigging)** Avatars can be inspected in **X-ray/skeleton view**. They are rigged with **biomechanical joints**, enabling joint-by-joint adjustment based on pose or fit needs. - **Avatar measurements (digital measuring tape)** Yellow lines represent a digital tape measure. Instead of guessing, students can view **precise industry-standard points of measure** directly on the 3D body. Students can verify avatar dimensions while grading patterns to maintain mathematical accuracy. - **Avatar poses (for dynamic presentation)** Because avatars have joints, they can be posed using **preset pose options** for more dynamic final portfolio presentations.

When This Workshop Took Place: Apr 10, 2026

Who This Workshop is For: Academic (Faculties & Students)

In this session from CLO's Academic Webinar Series, designed to bridge the gap between the classroom and the digital transformation in the global fashion industry, you'll learn how to work with avatars, create patterns from scratch, and bring garments to life in CLO simulation environment.
This session was conducted for academics (professors & instructors) and was also open to students to join and learn together.
Whether you're a fashion student, educator, or industry professional new to digital pattern making, this webinar walks you through every foundational step: from customizing your avatar's measurements to drafting, tracing, and constructing a basic bodice block entirely within CLO.

📌 What You'll Learn:
How to set up and customize avatars using Avatar Editor and Avatar Joints
How to take accurate body measurements (Basic Tape, Surface Tape, Linear, and Height)
How to navigate CLO's 2D Pattern Window
How to import and trace physical pattern pieces into digital patterns
How to use pattern drafting tools: French curves, rulers, fold lines, offset outlines, and more
How to construct a basic bodice block from real paper patterns

🧵 Part of an ongoing webinar series covering the full CLO workflow: Avatar → Pattern → Sew → Design Ideation → Materials → Production Ready.
